Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start […]
content: Today on Decoder , I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1. Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet. But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it . So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know. Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to Decoder . Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay. I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it? It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time. In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see. So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing. It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days. It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself. I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about. I actually just want to start at the really big picture. You run a thing called Tokenomics. I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people. I look at Anthropic and where it could go. I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue. Where does that money come from? Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues. I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . It’s so interesting. Today, because even the scale we’re at is $120 billion of ARR between the two leading labs, it’s still an extremely narrow market. The top 1 percent of customers are the ones that are spending $50,000 to $100,000 per employee. Your broader Fortune 500 or Global 2000, which typically do a lot of IT spend, isn’t spending much. A lot of the spending, especially at Anthropic, is coding-specific. It’s almost a single vertical company. We look in the future to 2027, you think to this broader adoption and white collar work. This typical enterprise Q4 budgeting season, we actually haven’t gone through with one of these labs yet in any meaningful way because their ARR did really start to accelerate until the beginning of the year. We think of other cases like cyber, which can be similar to coding, where these are eight-figure-plus contracts with leading enterprises that can scale very quickly due to all the cybersecurity incidents we’re seeing. You get to other verticals like bio. To get to $1 trillion, we do have to move to some of that white collar work, where it goes from AI augmentation to labor saving or replacement in some areas. You look at things like Microsoft’s buyout offers to employees as an example of this , but there’s no wealth of other verticals that they can get into and really start to move the needle. This is the single biggest question I have, not just about the S-1, but the entire industry. I would understand that if there are one or two leading labs. There are two big companies that have a technology that can automate a whole bunch of things. We will see how well that automation goes sector by sector, but there are not just two leading labs. There are quite a few of them. There are open weight models. I’ve heard from a lot of CEOs who are very nervous about giving all their data to an OpenAI or Anthropic and they would like to run some things on-prem. There are law firms running on-prem AI now, which is the funniest turn in maybe all of history. How do you see that playing out? Because so much of the pressure on this S-1 was the numbers themselves, which I want to talk about, but then there’s the external pressure of, “You’ve got to grow and growth is not as short.” So how do you see all of that playing out? It’s very interesting because when we look at coding today, for example — and I think we saw this in Q3 with OpenAI kind of catching up — there are areas of coding where there are very low switching costs, and I can just move between that. What we hear from enterprises and maybe, too, on the OpenAI side — obviously I think they somewhat botched the Fable release, and the lack of zero data retention is why we saw some of the slowdown. That’s something they can fix with Fable 5.5 and maybe drive more enterprise adoption there. That’s a huge thing for enterprises when we talk with them. We definitely see enterprises now, and more so, too, a lot of the AI natives, doing custom training and post-training on open weight models, and then running either their inference off of that or even their products for internal or external use cases. Obviously, DeepMind at Google and [Meta Superintelligence Labs] are very well-funded labs that have pretty similar training compute capacity, and they’re bringing on a ton of it. Not even to mention SpaceX as well, with what Elon said on [about] 10 net new gigawatts next year and half of that is the long-term internal use case. In the first half of the year, Anthropic ran away with it. They were 90 percent of the industry’s net new ARR. We saw in Q3 that OpenAI was probably actually the majority of industry net new ARR. Open-source has grown from probably $1 billion of token inference costs, ARR, in Q1 to $10 billion-plus here in Q3. So yes, the industry’s gotten much more competitive, but there are all these new use cases, too, and some of these verticalized use cases are really where we’re going to see the growth going forward. Because it’s obvious coding isn’t going to power us to even triple from here. It’s interesting. The concept is called Tokenomics. You run that practice alongside another co-lead at SemiAnalysis. Explain what it is because to me it’s such a smart way of thinking about, “We’re going to put some money in and maybe we’ll get some money out.” I think of it as the unit economics [of AI], or even just the broader idea — everything from a macro- to microeconomics of running an AI business or even looking at AI demand. So we cover the hyperscalers, now some of the neoclouds as well in a separate product. But then just the AI labs, too. For investors, or just people that are interested in the business, Anthropic had negative 94 percent gross margins on inference two years ago. Now they have a positive 85 percent margin, and people don’t understand how they allocate compute. How do we think about the inference business model? Part of that gross margin conversation is the revenue per megawatt in inference. Why are all companies that are running inference seeing massive gains in inference and compute efficiency? So we try to model out these businesses and obviously when Anthropic was private, we’re dealing with information we can get from the press and things like that. But now that we have concrete audited numbers, it’s easy to explain the unit economics of this. And also how the businesses differ. OpenAI is a much different business than Anthropic just in both their consumption versus subscription and then historical weight versus consumer versus enterprise. [We are] trying to understand across the demand level the economics of these businesses. Several years ago when I talked to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about the cost of inference, I said, “How are you ever going to make money?” He was just very clear. He said, “If there’s one thing Google’s good at, it’s bringing this stuff down the cost curve.” It was a very blunt answer. I understand how Google can do it. They make their own chips. Anthropic is running on everyone else’s clouds. The core part of the S-1 is how much they’ve committed to spend on other people’s clouds: SpaceXAI, Google, Amazon. Where does their efficiency come from? There’s really token throughput. They have a very diverse chip fleet. Between Trainiums, TPUs, and GPUs, across all of those, we see a ton of token efficiencies. Token throughput, for example, on Trainium chips is up 5x to 10x year-over-year right now. Dealing with both the hardware level efficiencies and the software — and how the model interacts with the hardware — there are a lot of token throughput gains where if you’re doing X tokens per second, now you’re doing five or 10 times that just a year later. What they’ll tell you is they see continued compute efficiencies as well going forward. Max Kan, who co-leads Tokenomics model with me at SemiAnalysis, and I have even published some research on this. Right now, if Anthropic’s at $65 million of revenue per inference megawatt, this was mid-teens last year at this time. What we’ve said on maybe Opus 5.5 on a [Nvidia] Blackwell, you can get to $100 to $120 million of revenue per megawatt. The big thing here is they’re paying on average now just a little over $10 million per megawatt in [cost of goods sold], or just in compute costs. What you can do with those margins is then reinvest in training. People don’t realize this, but only about 30 percent of the compute is actually in inference-serving revenue. The rest is for experimentation and research, training models, and post-training models. So there’s a lot of compute that is building the next model and that’s more of the R&D side and where you actually get your returns and defensibility in this business. Actually, what I was expecting to see in the S-1 was that dynamic play out much more strongly — that Anthropic makes a bunch of money selling the models they have now and there are more customers in the future for the models they have now. That’s going to throw off a whole bunch of margin. And then, because it is Anthropic and they think they’re building a digital god, they’re going to train the next models as much as they can. That is a very particular Anthropic story. The company is chasing AGI. The people who work there will happily tell you that in the S-1 that Claude might be conscious and this could all go to hell. Anthropic is a very unique company in its conception of itself. But you don’t really see that dynamic playing out in the S-1. They’re managing their training costs against their inference margin pretty well. Do you see that going up or changing in any way? I agree. Long term, and we’ve even said this internally, they want to actually increase the percentage of training. If you believe you’re building a digital god or going towards AGI, and as long as you have the gross margins of 85 percent-plus on inference to do so, you can. They’ve grown a lot faster than they thought, and they didn’t expect to be at 11 percent non-gap EBITA margins. They’d love to be closer to zero, or even below that if they could get that compute and allocate it towards training and continue to see these compute efficiencies. They’ve messaged that, too, to investors in the roadshow. You can look at this S-1 and just the curve of profitability over the last few years and how little cash they burned to get to this point and you can say, “This is a good business model, but we’re going towards AGI. Don’t expect the margin leverage we’re seeing to continue to this level, even though long-term margins can be quite a bit higher.” There are some real shades of Amazon there. Jeff Bezos famously told investors he wasn’t going to make money until he could make a lot of money. Obviously, Amazon and Anthropic have a lot of back and forth. Maybe there’s some family resemblance there. But I’m curious, there’s a point of model capability that would allow you to go into more verticals than just coding, right? We might be at it now. The idea of capability overhang exists, the idea that the models we have today could go and take over bio research. They’re taking over mathematics today. There’s a point at which the smartest business decision is to stop training and to just sell your profitable model into more and more companies. Anthropic as a public company will face that pressure. Do you think they’re organized or structured to fend it off? Yeah, I think they’re structured well. With some of the voting stock in areas like that, they definitely are. We’ve seen this in tech before and even publicly when Mark Zuckerberg has made these decisions before to invest heavily. It didn’t always pay off. I just want to point out, it didn’t always pay off. Yeah, it did not always pay off. Although you and I technically are in the metaverse right now, by some definition. [Laughs] Right. But I think that’s something, and there’s an interesting number in the S-1 that 80 percent of revenue in the last three months comes from models released in the last six months. So then you say, “Okay, 20 percent of the models are like Opus 4.5 in earlier versions.” One thing going forward is that if you’re a frontier model company, you always need to be at the frontier and it’s incredibly competitive. Wait, can I ask a really dumb question about that? Yeah. Why? I think the heart of my curiosity about the industry right now is if you enabled some bleeding-edge technology that could revolutionize the entire world, at some point, the most profitable thing to do is to just go play it out in all the different verticals, right? It’s not to go make the next one. It’s actually to run an efficient model in legal services and medicine and wherever else that there hasn’t been diffusion of AI yet. This idea that you always have to be at the frontier, that Anthropic always has to be competing with Google and OpenAI and whoever else, I get it from their self-conception. But from a business point of view, an AI-enabled business is going to throw out more money and spend more money with me, the AI provider, and that isn’t necessarily related to being at the frontier. There are a few portions of that. For new verticals, and this is very cyber specific, if an adversary is using a frontier model, you need to be defending with a frontier model. Fair enough. When we talk to some enterprises, it’s not like an email summary where I can run that on open source or Sonnet. There are just certain verticals where having… [For example,] if you were in a legal case as a defendant, would you be okay if your lawyer was using a non-frontier model if the prosecution— [Laughs] I got bad news for you about what’s going on in the legal market right now. The competitive dynamics do dictate that. I think from a go-forward perspective, we’ve seen this with open source too catching up in one point, but the demand will be there. [SemiAnalysis CEO] Dylan [Patel] says this a lot. The demand will always be there for frontier intelligence, especially in competitive industries. And there are certain tasks, as you go towards more labor replacement versus labor augmentation, where that also is the case. At the same time, they are getting more vertical. If you go look at job postings or what they’re hiring for, they’re putting out more of these SKUs and areas, and there’s a lot of beta testing going on like Claude for financial services, Claude for legal, their cyber program. They’re giving away 25,000 of credits per month for people in their cyber program. That’ll be a huge SKU for them in 2027. Those verticalized areas and then ones that are specifically where you need to be… It’s more adversarial, I should say, or competitive, are the main reasons why. But we can both agree there are areas like email summary and work that definitely doesn’t need to happen [at the frontier]. I’ll just make a dumb comparison to the iPhone. It’s iPhone season. I just reviewed the iPhone Duo. Apple kept the iPhone looking the same for several years now. They build all of the tooling for the new iPhone and then they just reuse it for two or three or four models to get all the value out of that investment back before they move on to the next thing. Apple puts out a new iPhone, and it keeps selling the old iPhone for a while to get more value out of that investment and that development program. The AI industry does not seem to be doing that. All of their emphasis is on developing the next new thing, deprecating the old thing pretty fast, and moving you onto the new expensive product, while at the same time they’re building the next new expensive product. At some point it feels like that will rationalize, that there will be something that is worth just collecting margin from while they go invest in the new thing. I just can’t figure out where Anthropic sits in that cycle. I mean, we do see this. Open source token volumes are picking up and there’s a lot of areas, yes, where the open source models have become good enough. I think on a go-forward basis, you’re like, “Okay, was that because of distillation?” And then the frontier labs have some defensibility actually going forward. I think when we talk to clients, it’s also about how we actually think about frontier versus open source. So something like a Sonnet type model, if you want to do the iPhone 18 versus the SE type analogy. We do see that dynamic, and obviously with open source, it’s a question of how much that can take. Two, because we’re so early in these verticals, we don’t know what’s going to be fully agentic. There’s no human in the loop where the harness actually has, I should say, some value and defensibility to it. The big area I’d look at here, especially when we talk to enterprises today, is only the coders are allowed to use the frontier models at a lot of these enterprises. If you’re a non-coder, some of these companies just limit you to Sonnet, if you’re an Anthropic customer. That’s reflective of how management views and wants to budget for this, what frontier intelligence is actually worth to them in certain areas. In my financial analyst brain, Claude could not build a good financial model six months ago. It’s getting better if you connect it to the right areas, but we’ve gone from something like, “I needed a junior analyst six months ago,” to, “Maybe I don’t as much anymore,” and then, “Will I have a full junior analyst at my disposal anytime or multiple pretty quickly, if I have unlimited token budget?” We just look at that across every vertical and major job category. The time horizon in each of those categories is going to be different. That’s just one of the bigger questions I have: How quickly do they get to where they think they can go? I want to dig in on some of the numbers here. The one that jumped out in all of the comment sections on all of the forums and all of our articles yesterday was $80 billion. Anthropic lost $80 billion [in the first half of 2026]. That is related to a technical charge. Can you just explain the $80 billion? Because it doesn’t seem particularly relevant to the revenue and profits they’re talking about. Yeah, it’s a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much and they’ve issued warrants or convertible notes. You have to account for that in your balance sheet. It’s just a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much since they issued these warrants and notes. That’s something you would always back out. You can argue on stuff like stock-based compensation. Should we really be thinking about that on a non-GAAP cash basis? Because it’s non-cash, if I just hand employees shares, I have to account for that on my income statement, but I’m not actually handing them pure cash out of my bank balance. So it’s not an area like that. It gets the accounting, the high level. If you don’t know accounting, it looks bad, but it’s because they’ve grown so much and their valuation has gone up so much. Some of the argument here about that charge is that Amazon was the other party there. Obviously Amazon’s very happy because Anthropic is buying a ton of AWS and sure they’re happy the valuation has gone up, but over time Amazon’s going to get diluted this way. That’s part of the dynamic there. Anthropic is going to obviously IPO. They’re going to put a bunch of shares in the market. It’s very clear that over time they will issue more shares to raise more money. It doesn’t seem like they’re going to stop wanting to raise money anytime soon. How are you thinking about that in terms of just investment into a company like Anthropic, that your valuation might be going up, but your actual ownership stake might be getting diluted over time? The deals have always been very creatively structured.  The number is they’ve actually only burned $10 billion of cash. They have $120 billion-plus of cash and marketable securities in the balance sheet today, and post-IPO, probably another $100 billion. It’s a great deal for both parties. They only really rent compute. It’s not like they have these massive capital outlays or even rent-to-own. You can make some arguments about certain accounting and there are these massive compute commitment obligations and that’s technically future debt, or that is sitting somewhat off balance sheet essentially. But from a dilution perspective, all tech companies dilute. Are they going to need to raise another $100 billion of debt or equity at some point? Possibly. Can they continue to creatively structure and finance future compute buildouts? Probably as well. I know there’s been a lot of angst about the future of compute financing and data center financing in the last few weeks. But if you’re Anthropic, if you’re a major lab, a hyperscaler or Broadcom or Nvidia that are backstopping a lot of these deals, that’s probably not going to change anytime soon. So I’m not particularly worried. As an equity investor, would I be worried about getting super diluted? I don’t think so. If you believe in this long-term AGI bull case and that Anthropic is going to be a leader in this, that probably shouldn’t worry you. You’re probably looking at a $10 trillion-plus business. They can outrun dilution at that point. Let’s talk about the compute commitments. I saw at least one analysis saying over the next 10 years, it’s $800 billion-plus in commitments to the various hyperscalers and neoclouds. That’s a lot. You’re saying that they don’t have that much money. They haven’t even spent that much money yet. Do you see them generating the revenues to pay off those commitments? Yeah. I think when people look at the headline commitments, the $500 to $600 billion number over 7 to 10 years, let’s call it, what they’re paying for compute today actually isn’t that many gigawatts. If you think about their spending right now, on average they’re close to $11 million per megawatt in spend, or $11 billion per gigawatt. If you take that back to the annual level and say, “Okay, the $520 billion number is over 70 years, for example, that’s really not that many gigawatts and they’re going to be well beyond…” When they get to something like 20 gigawatts, the future compute commitments that they’re running essentially is going to be well into the trillions. So yes, they are going to have the revenue to do so. It’s more about how much revenue they are going to have relative to how much compute. Two, the compute efficiency equation. If they keep getting a lot more revenue out of every inference megawatt, how much do you really want to invest in training and take margins to zero from a rental perspective? Because you can get to something where even 80 percent to 85 percent of their fleet is just on training and research at these kinds of margins. The revenue is going to scale pretty well. They’re not in any dire situations there. Unless we realize all this revenue disappears or people churn. It’s not like they have to hit a trillion dollars of revenue extremely, extremely quickly to achieve all this and pay for this. Unless you’re trying to build digital God and unless it doesn’t diffuse across the economy as fast as everyone wants it to. Those are bets, right? They’re huge bets. The numbers you look at, if you’re really bullish on this ramp into the digital economy, is Anthropic saying within their Fortune 500 customers, they have 50 percent of the Fortune 500 and that is just 0.1 percent of their total customers’ operating expenses. When you look at that on a per user basis, it’s like $8 a month if you believe OpEx doesn’t include the cost of goods sold. If you believe they include the cost of goods sold, it’s sub-$50 per month. They said the same thing. Of the top 5 percent of Claude Code users, they’re spending $18,000 a year on average, the top 5 percent of users. Their non-Claude Code users spend under $75 a month, well under $75. There’s this huge opportunity, especially when we talk to enterprises and these traditional buyers of IT software. Penetration is extremely low in traditional white collar work. That’s the big point, too, that there is a large ramp period here of both seats adoption and usage. You can make arguments of who’s going to win in this, but it’s obvious the frontier labs are going to get some portion of this and it’s going to be pretty material to net new ARR next year. One of the things that’s really interesting about that is we talk about the frontier labs, we talk about the hyperscalers — Anthropic has a lot of wild risk factors in this S-1, including that Claude might be conscious and kill us all. But one of the most direct and maybe easiest to understand is that AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are both suppliers and competitors in some real way, particularly Google. And they say, “These relationships could turn.” They have a big relationship with SpaceXAI. Elon Musk is going to train Grok. They’re going to compete with SpaceXAI at some point. That relationship might become precarious. As you say, they’re only renting their compute. At some point, the market might force them to own more of their compute because their own competitors don’t want to lease their capacity to the leading company. How do you see that playing out? We definitely see both OpenAI and Anthropic going more direct and not owning the compute, but more rent-to-own, or going through an SPV as some financial sponsors do and producing the compute more directly versus renting. There are two points to this. Google, from one perspective, is also selling its external chips to customers and saying, “We don’t care to monetize this within Google Cloud or even allocate the share… If you think we’re very chip-constrained, we don’t even care that these are going to DeepMind or internal GCP compute for us to monetize. We’re just willing to become a chip seller.” Anthropic loves TPUs and there are 3.5 to 4 gigawatts-plus, and probably more in the pipeline, in terms of orders there of Anthropic buying these chips directly to then rent. So yes, the market is good. Wait, it’s not buying them directly to rent. So they’re buying them into a neocloud? Yeah, they buy them through an SPV, or the SPV buys them and then they rent it from the SPV. Got it. Okay. Even within Google Cloud or AWS or Foundry, Anthropic is massive — 48 percent of their business comes through the Bedrock Foundry and Vertex where people are paying through their existing cloud relationship to access these models. They’re not even talking to Anthropic. You don’t have to interact with the Anthropic sales force. You mentioned this earlier. This marketing channel where Anthropic gets a rev share. Right. If you’re AWS and you’re saying, “I’m running Anthropic compute for, let’s say, $10 million per megawatt, but now I’m getting 16 percent of $65 billion-a-megawatt plus the compute costs as well,” so we’re seeing margins at all the clouds go up right now. Part of it is CPU utilization is going up because of all the coding and then some on the [reinforcement learning] side, but these token-as-a-service businesses as we call them — so AWS Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Gemini Agent Enterprise platform, which is formerly Vertex — are actually massively increasing the margins on AI at these clouds. They’re benefiting as well when shareholders are giving them credit for this recently. In Q2, both Azure and AWS had extremely, extremely strong quarters, AWS specifically, on the back of Anthropic’s growth on Bedrock. Do you think that will keep Amazon from ever wanting to train its own frontier models? They’re doing a good job of letting AWS be the infrastructure for everybody else, but they’re one of the only big tech companies that hasn’t felt the insecurity of not having their own models. Yeah, it’s interesting. Amazon is very happy to serve a wide variety of customers and they have very little [frontier capability]. When we look at our estimates of training compute, they have the least of any hyperscaler, except maybe Oracle. It doesn’t seem like there’s much strategy there. I know Microsoft in the last two quarters has been talking about it a little more. AWS on the call has been talking about it a little more, but it’s not huge. They’re not doing it to the same extent that Meta is or trying to be competitive here or even Google with Gemini. Especially someone like Dylan will tell you, if you’re not trying to compete at the frontier, there’s really not a place for you, especially if you’re only dedicating a few hundred megawatts internally. One, internal use case is like serving Amazon retail, but then two, training. There are a lot of commitments to make to be good at this. It’s a conversation for a different day, but I look at these Microsoft job cuts and I see it as the glimmer of evidence that they’re going to try to compete in the future. They obviously got burned pretty badly by OpenAI. Yeah. They have, in the new agreement that they signed, the right to monetize OpenAI models for essentially not paying OpenAI anything within that agreement. They’re going to have some interesting things ahead where they monetize the OpenAI models or even through Microsoft 365 Cowork and Copilot applications where they’re not paying OpenAI anything for a frontier model. The other dynamic here, and you brought it up earlier, is over the last few weeks, there’s just been a lot of stress about neoclouds — whether they will succeed, whether they will fail. I think Elon Musk said there will be a guppy-like extinction event , which is just a brutal metaphor to use to describe a bunch of data centers. But this is a bunch of circular financing and Nvidia stood a bunch of them up and maybe the hyperscalers are just going to run away with it. Maybe Anthropic’s demand, because maybe they will want to own more of their own compute because renting it is precarious in all these ways. What do you make of the neoclouds? Do you think they’re going to survive the market actually shaking itself out as these companies go public? Elon obviously has some incentive to say neoclouds are going to be extinct. ClusterMAX said something else and just does amazing ratings of the neoclouds . There are a lot of neoclouds that are ex-crypto miners that are not good businesses and are not good at operating clusters. I just want to point out CoreWeave is an ex-crypto mining company, right? Yeah. I don’t mean CoreWeave, but there are others further down the list. CoreWeave, Nebius, and anyone that has backing or backstops from one of the major labs, hyperscalers, Nvidia, or Broadcom is going to be okay. It’s that longer tail. Hyperscalers have been 65 percent of CapEx and net new compute brought online. There’s 35 percent of the market that doesn’t have the balance sheets that the hyperscalers have. Both Google and Meta have recently raised or announced they’re going to raise. When we look at the big four hyperscalers, they don’t actually need to raise that money over the next two years, even though CapEx is growing from $1.2 to $2 trillion pretty quickly. But for a lot of these other neoclouds, if you don’t have that sort of backing, I think it is very hard, even right now, and becoming extremely difficult if you don’t have the backing or backstops from those players to keep building compute. It’s a very, very tough financing market. One of the things I think is really interesting about Elon in particular talking about neoclouds dying and obviously hyping up his own data center business is he’s trying to put them in space and to get away from the backlash in the United States around data centers in particular. We have a lot of coverage about data center backlash in the United States, it is slowing down a lot of projects. But at the rate we’re going, if you think the neoclouds are shaky, you might actually end up abandoning a bunch of GPUs and half-built data centers or have them tied up in financing agreements where they can’t be lit up. What do you make of that? Do you think we actually just need to go to space? Or do you think the market is going to rationalize and actually take advantage of all the compute that is currently allocated but not being used? We’ll rationalize more so. The market is very good at finding places to put chips here on the ground. Politically, we’ll see what happens next week with midterms and the fallout from that. Obviously, there are some very large sites that still have massive permitting problems. There’s the entire power equation as we look towards next year. The data centers will be built. There will be a method to get these built. The biggest thing — and the hyperscale CFOs have said this — from an overbuilt perspective and on a relative basis, it’s pretty cheap to build the data center shell. What they can do if they overbuild is they’re going to say, “We’re just not going to take delivery of the chip. We’re not going to buy chips. We’re not going to fill them up.” They’ll just sit empty and chipless. But the majority of the spend is on the chip side. So if we do end up in a place where we’re actually oversupplied from a data center perspective, I know that’s a little bit different. It’s the exact opposite of what the question was. They have said that from an ROI perspective. This comes back to that larger question of whether we are still going to be super supply constrained. A lot of people now, especially in the last three weeks, are talking about, “Are we in this massive glut of compute as we look towards 2028 actually?” Because the same thing we talked about from Anthropic going from negative 94 percent margins to positive 85 percent and compute efficiencies mean as you bring on more inference megawatts that are making a lot more revenue per megawatt, all else SQL, you need less compute. So it’s a question of whether we we going to have enough revenue in 2028 to justify the ROI on $2 trillion plus of CapEx. This is why I spent so much time asking about capability overhang and how good the models are today, because you can see some competitor that is less idealistic about AGI saying, “Actually, we’re going to do a bunch of forward-deployed engineers in all of these verticals where they haven’t taken advantage of AI and sell them high-margin inference because we’ll automate big chunks of their business and they’ll see the return.” Right now, a bunch of the Fortune 500 has not seen a return on AI spending . So if you’re actually just better at customer service and deployment and productizing the model, you might get way ahead of where Anthropic needs to be because they’re still thinking about AGI every single minute of every single day. I look at Dario standing next to Marc Benioff at Dreamforce and that dude does not want to be there right now. He wants to be thinking about the machine god. There’s something there where you can just see competitors coming up with an open source model and saying, “We’re actually going to productize this and we will actually take the revenue that everyone else is depending on.” Yeah, it’s extremely, extremely interesting. In the interim, that’s why it is getting more verticalized because you need something to bridge AGI where it just fully does the job, you need something to bridge the actual model today. [Laughs] Yeah. We’ll just take that for granted. To get there, you need some bridges of where it sits with the actual end user at some point. Everything is going to come down to this: Is there going to be some timing or adoption mismatch where we just don’t get the revenue at a certain point of time to justify that chase of “train and compute towards AGI”? That’s a risk. The other risk we look at is whether we get more models at the frontier even at the open source that are as competitive in coding, where token pricing across the frontier needs to be taken down, because like I mentioned earlier, there are lower switching costs. Even at SemiAnalysis, we went from 95 percent or 90 percent-plus of our usage at the end of Q2 was on Anthropic’s models down to 70 percent after the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT 5.6 and Astra. And then with Opus 5.5, it’s gone back to 90 percent-plus roughly. It does come back. Even the base of revenue today — and they’ve said that we have net revenue retention of 900 percent, so they’re seeing this massive, massive growth. This isn’t a traditional software business like ServiceNow or Workday, where you have just an incredible logo or gross retention of 95 percent to 98 percent and customers sign these nice three-year contracts, they never churn, they add some seats, and maybe they adopt another product that is being upsold. This is purely consumption. The other portion was the 20 percent drop in the last two weeks of the year versus the prior two weeks last year in token spend, because of the holiday season. You’re not going to do work code stuff, you’re not going to be coding for work during the holidays. This is extremely, extremely pure consumption business, even different from how we think about Snowflake or Datadog today in public markets. Obviously, Anthropic is not the only company that’s going to have an IPO. OpenAI is right next to them. They’ve delayed theirs. You mentioned earlier Anthropic is much more enterprise focused. I think OpenAI for a long time thought that Google wouldn’t react to them and they would just take the search business away and everything would be fine. Google obviously reacted for better or worse. Search is now AI Overviews. Looking at the Anthropic S-1, what are you looking ahead to with OpenAI? Because they are a more consumer facing company. OpenAI was 60-40 consumer, 60 percent consumer and 40 percent enterprise at the end of Q1. That didn’t flip for the first time until January or August to be enterprise focused. What they’ll tell you is enterprise business — because it was so consumer and subscription focused, this consumption business that’s 80 percent of Anthropic’s revenue — didn’t take off until a release of 5.6 and then with Astra. Those are really great models. OpenAI took the majority of actual net new ARR in Q3, but it’s going to take some time because what’s been in the Wall Street Journal , like negative 100 percent EBITA margins versus we’re seeing positive 11 percent here. There are some differences, some pretty big differences, in the business model where they just don’t monetize at the same rate that Anthropic does. That’s a little bit because the business makeup — the verticals, that consumer-versus-enterprise split — and that’s changing. What they’ll tell you is they see a really good Q4 and they have a much stronger enterprise sales function than Anthropic has. I expect them to come up, but I don’t think the financials are going to look as good as this even when they drop their S-1 maybe in early 2027. Do you think that’s why they delayed it? To get their financials looking better? Yeah, I think OpenAI had a really strong Q3 . Enterprise grew 100 percent quarter-over-quarter versus the total business which was 77 percent. You get another strong quarter of enterprise here. If Opus 5.5 didn’t take a ton of share, that would put OpenAI in a much better position to tell the story. There are some other turns here between now and when Anthropic actually goes public. They’re going to do a roadshow. There’ll be some pricing events. What are you looking for from Anthropic? They did an investor day two or three weeks ago where they did give some more color. I think they’ll walk through why Q3 was so weak. Meta was a very, very large customer, probably over 10 percent. What’s been publicly reported is they went from 60,000 Claude Code seats down to 30,000. These token volumes didn’t disappear, they just shifted into Meta’s internal models. Anthropic started cracking down on anti-distillation, and that was 5 percent of revenue prior. I think they said 5 percent to 7 percent of revenue in the S-1 and stuff against their terms of service. So what’s here on the roadshows is a lot of this October acceleration after Opus 5.5. We believe that they’re back on track. If they were doing $10 billion of net new ARR per month in Q2 and that fell down to $4 billion in Q3, that they’re getting back on that $8 billion to $10 billion pace here in Q4. People want to hear about these new verticals, specifically cyber. They’re doing some patching until they have that full cyber SKU rolled out, but they’re definitely monetizing cyber today for vulnerability code scanning. These are not small contracts, I should say, with existing customers. I think they’ll start to message what the 2027 ARR growth path looks like. The other thing too is expectations management, keeping numbers low enough, not talking about AGI as much. [Laughs] It’s hard to do expectation management when your risk factors are like, “We could pose an existential risk to all of humanity.” [Laughs] Right. And so saying you do that — you’re going to achieve AGI at some point, you’re going to replace everyone’s jobs — but then trying to keep numbers low enough for Q4 and to have this massive beat the first quarter you become public and have a decent guide for 2027, it’ll be a nice mix of seesawing between that long-term vision and short-term expectations management. There’s a lot going on. Joey, this has been great. We’re going to have to have you back as these companies barrel towards actually being public and their economics become much more visible. content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time —Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability . ​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.  Here’s what needs to change . Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century. Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming . —James Temple This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday. Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries  Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer. The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels. Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise . —Alexander C. title: STAT+: New atlas of colorectal tumors sheds light on why cancers in young people are more dangerous
summary: A new atlas of colorectal tumors sheds light on why cancers in young people are more dangerous.
content: For years, scientists have struggled to elucidate key biological differences between early onset colorectal cancer, typically in patients under the age of 50, and older patients. They’ve long believed that these cancers must be biologically distinct, since younger patients tend to be far more difficult to treat. They’re often diagnosed at later stages with tumors with more aggressive features. “Their survival, especially for the very youngest patients under the age of 35, may actually not be as good as somebody in their 40s or someone in their 60s, despite receiving more aggressive treatment and being at baseline healthier,” said Kimmie Ng, a colorectal cancer researcher and director of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center. “So we have always believed tumors may be biologically different.” On Thursday, Ng published a new study in Nature Medicine that may help illuminate critical differences between older and younger colorectal cancer patients. With 189 tumors, it’s the largest biological database — what researchers call a single cell atlas — of colorectal cancer tumors in patients ranging from their 20s to their 90s. The atlas, along with the technology Ng and her colleagues used, should help researchers control for variables that confounded studies in the past. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…

content: Today, as part of its commitment to strengthening health information systems and improving health[1], especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO announced a new approach to improving access to life-saving data: the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the urgent need for timely and reliable data to drive strategic health action. Too many countries still lack both the infrastructure to routinely gather health data and the analytical capacity to use these data for effective health actions and emergency response. “Countries must be able to measure progress to make progress,” said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. “Particularly during COVID-19, reliable data is the best way to coordinate response efforts and improve health in all areas.” Accurate health data are necessary to understand specific country needs in order to improve health and save lives. Data also helps direct scarce resources to where they are needed most. The SCORE (Survey, Count, Optimize, Review, Enable) Technical Package aims to improve the availability of timely, reliable, validated, and comparable health data. For the first time in a single, harmonized package, it represents all the key elements for optimized health information system performance. Simply put, SCORE will help governments around the globe set benchmarks and improve standards in healthcare. In response to the challenges of data availability highlighted in the WHO World Health Statistics 2020 report, SCORE includes more than 90 universally-accepted tools and standards for health information systems strengthening. “Using data to inform public health priorities and strategies has never been more important,” said Dr Kelly Henning, Director of Public Health Programs at Bloomberg Philanthropies[2]. “The SCORE Technical Package provides country governments around the world with high-quality, essential technical guidance so that countries can strengthen their own data systems.” WHO is proud to partner with the Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative to deliver this timely resource to countries.   Below are some examples of how SCORE can improve individual lives and communities: The birth of a child is registered so they can access essential health services, attend school, and apply for a passport; A death is registered with cause-of-death accurately captured so that policy-makers have a better understanding of all-cause and COVID-specific mortality and associated risk factors and implement programs and policies to save lives; Health data are disaggregated by age, sex and cause of death to illustrate the root causes of health disparities and help direct resources to the most vulnerable groups such as those who do not speak the local language or face stigma and discrimination in their community; Health facilities have the capacity to regularly measure the quality of their services, workforce and patient data and can make a compelling case for increased funding to national and international stakeholders; Health data are integrated with other sectors so that social determinants of health such as pollution, sanitation and nutrition are addressed to reduce the overall burden of disease. The package's initial release includes two documents: SCORE Essential Interventions – including an overview of health information systems, underlying elements, and indicators to assess progress with sample actions; and SCORE Tools and Standards -- including resources to address critical health data gaps and strengthen country health data. “We must keep score to save lives. WHO is committed to working with countries and partners to rapidly scale up capacity for data collection and use in order to improve policy and performance,” added Dr Samira Asma, Assistant Director-General for Data, Analytics and Delivery for Impact at WHO. “We must act now to invest in statistical systems in countries, respond to this pandemic and meet the SDGs and the Triple Billion targets. Our window of opportunity is closing, and we cannot wait to address data gaps. Data use to address country needs has to be a priority today.” Country-owned, disaggregated data will be essential for more resilient and sustainable health systems going forward. COVID-19 is both a wake-up call and a stark reminder of the challenges we still have to address. But it is also an opportunity to build back better through solidarity, information-sharing and collaboration. SCORE is one example of how a collaborative approach can benefit countries by providing a common set of tools based on shared standards. This package is designed to be practical, actionable and flexible. We will only be successful in combatting COVID-19 if we work together. Future components of the SCORE Technical Package are due to be released later this year, including the SCORE Assessment Instrument and global, regional and country status reports.  Together, these will provide a complete package of information to plan and monitor progress against national and subnational priorities as well as global targets. ----- [1] https://www.who.int/about/what-we-do/thirteenth-general-programme-of-work-2019---2023#:~:text=The%20Thirteenth%20General%20Programme%20of,health%20at%20the%20country%20leve [2] Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative provided funding to support the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package

title: WHO statement on notification of withdrawal of the United States
summary: WHO regrets the United States’ notification of withdrawal from WHO – a decision that makes both the United States and the world less safe. The notification of withdrawal raises issues that will be considered by the WHO Executive Board at its regular meeting starting on 2 February and by the World Health Assembly at its annual meeting in May 2026.
content: As a founding member of the World Health Organization (WHO), the United States of America has contributed significantly to many of WHO’s greatest achievements, including the eradication of smallpox, and progress against many other public health threats including polio, HIV, Ebola, influenza, tuberculosis, malaria, neglected tropical diseases, antimicrobial resistance, food safety and more. WHO therefore regrets the United States’ notification of withdrawal from WHO – a decision that makes both the United States and the world less safe. The notification of withdrawal raises issues that will be considered by the WHO Executive Board at its regular meeting starting on 2 February and by the World Health Assembly at its annual meeting in May 2026. WHO takes note of statements from the government of the United States that say WHO has “trashed and tarnished” and insulted it, and compromised its independence. The reverse is true. As we do with every Member State, WHO has always sought to engage with the United States in good faith, with full respect for its sovereignty. In its statements, the United States cited as one of the reasons for its decision, “WHO failures during the COVID-19 pandemic”, including “obstructing the timely and accurate sharing of critical information” and that WHO “concealed those failures”. While no organization or government got everything right, WHO stands by its response to this unprecedented global health crisis. Throughout the pandemic, WHO acted quickly, shared all information it had rapidly and transparently with the world, and advised Member States on the basis of the best available evidence. WHO recommended the use of masks, vaccines and physical distancing, but at no stage recommended mask mandates, vaccine mandates or lockdowns. We supported sovereign governments to make decisions they believed were in the best interests of their people, but the decisions were theirs. Immediately after receiving the first reports of a cluster of cases of “pneumonia of unknown cause” in Wuhan, China on 31 December 2019, WHO asked China for more information and activated its emergency incident management system. By the time the first death was reported from China on 11 January 2020, WHO had already alerted the world through formal channels, public statements and social media, convened global experts, and published comprehensive guidance for countries on how to protect their populations and health systems. When the WHO Director-General declared COVID-19 a public health emergency of international concern under the International Health Regulations on 30 January 2020 – the highest level of alarm under international health law – outside of China there were fewer than 100 reported cases, and no reported deaths. In the first weeks and months of the pandemic, the Director-General urged all countries repeatedly to take immediate action to protect their populations, warning that “the window of opportunity is closing”, “this is not a drill” and describing COVID-19 as “public enemy number one”. In response to the multiple reviews of the COVID-19 pandemic, including of WHO’s performance, WHO has taken steps to strengthen its own work, and to support countries to bolster their own pandemic preparedness and response capacities. The systems we developed and managed before, during and after the emergency phase of the pandemic, and which run 24/7, have contributed to keeping all countries safe, including the United States. The United States also said in its statements that WHO has “pursued a politicized, bureaucratic agenda driven by nations hostile to American interests”. This is untrue. As a specialized agency of the United Nations, governed by 194 Member States, WHO has always been and remains impartial and exists to serve all countries, with respect for their sovereignty, and without fear or favour. WHO appreciates the support and continued engagement of all its Member States, which continue to work within the framework of WHO to pursue solutions to the world’s biggest health threats, both communicable and noncommunicable. Most notably, WHO Member States last year adopted the WHO Pandemic Agreement, which once ratified will become a landmark instrument of international law to keep the world safer from future pandemics. Member States are now negotiating an annex to the WHO Pandemic Agreement, the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing system, which if adopted will promote rapid detection and sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential, and equitable and timely access to vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics. We hope that in the future, the United States will return to active participation in WHO. Meanwhile, WHO remains steadfastly committed to working with all countries in pursuit of its core mission and constitutional mandate: the highest attainable standard of health as a fundamental right for all people.

title: Timor-Leste certified malaria-free by WHO
summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) has certified Timor-Leste as malaria-free, a remarkable achievement for a country that prioritized the disease and embarked on a concerted, nation-wide response shortly after gaining independence in 2002. “WHO congratulates the people and government of Timor-Leste on this significant milestone,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-Genera
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has certified Timor-Leste as malaria-free, a remarkable achievement for a country that prioritized the disease and embarked on a concerted, nation-wide response shortly after gaining independence in 2002. “WHO congratulates the people and government of Timor-Leste on this significant milestone,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “Timor-Leste’s success proves that malaria can be stopped in its tracks when strong political will, smart interventions, sustained domestic and external investment and dedicated health workers unite.” With today’s announcement, a total of 47 countries and 1 territory have been certified as malaria-free by WHO. Timor-Leste is the third country to be certified in the WHO South-East Asia region, joining Maldives and Sri Lanka which were certified in 2015 and 2016 respectively. Certification of malaria elimination is granted by WHO when a country has proven, beyond reasonable doubt, that the chain of indigenous transmission has been interrupted nationwide for at least the previous three consecutive years. “We did it. Malaria has been one of our most relentless enemies – silent, persistent, and deadly. We lost too many lives to a disease that should be preventable. But our health workers never gave up, our communities held strong, and our partners, like WHO, walked beside us. From 223 000 cases to zero – this elimination honours every life lost and every life now saved. We must safeguard this victory with continued vigilance and community action to prevent malaria's re-entry,” said Dr Élia António de Araújo dos Reis Amaral, SH, Minister of Health, Government of Timor-Leste. A rapid shift from high burden country to malaria-free Since gaining independence in 2002, Timor-Leste has made remarkable strides in the fight against malaria – reducing cases from a peak of more than 223 000 clinically diagnosed cases in 2006 to zero indigenous cases from 2021 onwards. Timor-Leste’s success in eliminating malaria was driven by the Ministry of Health’s swift action in 2003 to establish the National Malaria Programme, a dedicated programme for planning, implementing, and monitoring malaria control efforts nationwide. With only two full-time officers initially, the programme was able to lay the foundation for progress early on through strong technical leadership, managerial capacity and attention to detail. Within a few years, the country introduced rapid diagnostic tests and artemisinin-based combination therapy as part of the National Malaria Treatment Guidelines and began distributing free long-lasting insecticide treated nets to communities most at risk. In 2009, with support from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, Timor-Leste scaled up nationwide vector control efforts through the distribution of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets and indoor residual spraying. Malaria diagnosis was also expanded using microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests at the point of care across all local health posts. Facing the challenges of severe shortages of health workers and doctors, Timor-Leste made investments and developed its three-tier health system – comprising national hospitals, reference hospitals, community health centers (CHCs), and health posts – to ensure most residents can access care within an hour's walk. Additionally, citizens are provided with free health services at the point of care, as part of the government’s policy on free universal health care. Monthly mobile clinics and community outreach programmes further enhance health services in rural areas. Timor-Leste’s success in combating malaria highlights the importance of country leadership and strong collaboration between the Ministry of Health, WHO, local communities, non-governmental organizations, donors, and multiple government sectors. A real-time integrated case-based surveillance system ensures rapid data collection and response, while trained health workers ensure timely detection and screening of malaria cases, including at borders. These integrated efforts have paved the way for the country to be officially certified malaria-free. "Timor-Leste’s malaria-free certification is a defining national triumph – driven by bold leadership, tireless efforts of health workers, and the resolve of its people. As a young nation, Timor-Leste stayed focused – testing, treating, and investigating swiftly. Ending transmission and maintaining zero deaths takes more than science; it takes grit. This victory protects generations, present and future, and shows what a determined country can achieve,” said Dr Arvind Mathur, WHO Representative to Timor-Leste.   Note to the editor WHO malaria-free certification The final decision on awarding a malaria-free certification is made by the WHO Director-General, based on a recommendation by the Technical Advisory Group on Malaria Elimination and Certification and validation from the Malaria Policy Advisory Group. More on WHO’s malaria-free certification process .

title: African Union and World Health Organization renew strategic partnership to drive impact and strengthen health systems in Africa
summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the African Union (AU) Commission renewed their longstanding strategic partnership today with the signing of an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva. This renewed agreement reaffirms the joint commitment to advancing health security, universal health coverage, and sustainable development acros
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the African Union (AU) Commission renewed their longstanding strategic partnership today with the signing of an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva. This renewed agreement reaffirms the joint commitment to advancing health security, universal health coverage, and sustainable development across the African continent at a time of unprecedented financial challenges in the global health landscape. It further underscores the African Union’s leadership in fostering collective action, inclusive partnerships, and regional resilience, and positions the Department of Health, Humanitarian Affairs, and Social Development of the AU Commission at the heart of the continent’s health policy implementation efforts. The agreement was signed by Her Excellency Ambassador Amma Adomaa Twum-Amoah, Commissioner for Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development, on behalf of His Excellency Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African Union Commission, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. It marks a defining moment for primary health care and universal health coverage. Commissioner Twum-Amoah emphasized the strategic importance of the agreement and the AU’s leadership in shaping Africa’s health landscape: “This Agreement marks a new chapter in AU–WHO cooperation. By working together more closely, we can better respond to the health needs of our populations and ensure that no one is left behind. The African Union values WHO’s central and leading role in global health and looks forward to deepening this strategic partnership in support of our shared goals. We need to move from budgeting for survival to planning for health sovereignty,” she added. Building on the foundation of the 2019 MoU, the renewed agreement streamlines and strengthens collaboration across all AU entities. It aligns efforts in support of Africa’s health priorities and sets the stage for enhanced cooperation between WHO and the AU. It also reaffirms WHO’s central technical and normative leadership role in global and regional health, and its commitment to supporting the AU and its institutions in achieving health-related Sustainable Development Goals. “This renewed agreement comes at a critical time, as cuts to bilateral aid imperil the health of millions in Africa,” said Dr Tedros. “It reflects our determination to translate our partnership into tangible results for the people of Africa, and support countries to leave behind the era of aid dependency and transition to sustainable self-reliance. We are proud to stand with the African Union in driving forward the health priorities of the continent.” The Memorandum outlines five key areas of collaboration: health systems strengthening : including regulatory harmonization, support for local pharmaceutical manufacturing, traditional medicine, domestic health financing, workforce development, and digital health innovation; reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child, and adolescent health (RMNCAH) : with continued support for the Campaign on Accelerated Reduction of Maternal Mortality in Africa (CARMMA Plus 2021–2030) and advancement of the reviewed Addis Ababa Declaration on Immunization (ADi); disease prevention and control : supporting the implementation of AU frameworks on communicable and noncommunicable diseases, including efforts to end AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria; eliminate neglected tropical diseases (NTDs); and address the burden of viral hepatitis in line with WHO strategies; nutrition and food security : strengthening the nutrition agenda through implementation of the Africa Nutrition Strategy 2015–2025 and related WHO strategies; and health in emergency settings : by strengthening joint responses to humanitarian crises, conflicts, and climate-related emergencies. The timing of the renewed agreement is significant. It reflects the African Union’s elevated voice in global health governance – bolstered by its G20 membership – and highlights WHO’s ongoing key role as a trusted technical and operational partner. The renewed MoU marks new momentum for regional and multilateral cooperation to address Africa’s most pressing health challenges and deliver meaningful, lasting results on the continent. title: Frank, in-depth discussion as Belgium and WHO map ahead priorities for collaboration
summary: In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies. The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and othe
content: In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies. The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape. The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe. "After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together." Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success. Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation. Universal Health Coverage (UHC) Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care. The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas. WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together". Looking into the future The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy. The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14 th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work. "We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism". content: The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy , well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond. KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
